hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? think of the last thing you really wanted to buy. how long did the glow last after it arrived?
options: same. this old hermit knew why.
lovely. maybe you already know this one.
that might say it all. listen.

steps.line: In an old Daoist story, Yao, a wise emperor of legend, went looking for a hermit named Xu You, who lived simply by a river.
“When the sun and moon are out, why keep the torches burning?” said Yao. “You are the sun. Please, take my empire.”

steps.q: An emperor offers a hermit the whole empire. What does Xu You do?
o: Agrees to advise, but not to rule
Takes it, then gives it away
steps.why: A flat no. And he explains it with a little bird. Zhuangzi’s hermits often say no to power.

steps.line: “The tailorbird builds its nest in the deep forest,” said Xu You, “but it uses no more than one branch.”
“The mole drinks from the river, but takes no more than a bellyful. Go home, my lord. I have no use for the empire.”

steps.q: Why does Xu You talk about a bird and a mole, instead of just saying no?
o: Every creature needs only so much
He’d rather live in a forest
steps.why: The bird needs its branch. The mole needs its drink. Neither needs the whole forest, or the whole river.

steps.q: Later tellings add one more thing Xu You did after the emperor left. What?
o: Washed out his ears in the river
steps.why: He washed his ears, as if the offer had dirtied them. One version adds a herdsman who wouldn’t let his ox drink that water downstream.

steps.line: In a later telling, Xu You was so unmoved by the offer that he went down to the river and washed out his ears.
steps.label: a later telling

steps.line: Today the forest fits in a shopping cart. The glow of the new thing fades, and the wanting walks on. Xu You stopped at one branch.
steps.label: today

steps.q: Your phone works fine, and a new one comes out. What’s the tailorbird’s question?
o: Does this one do what I need?
Can I afford the new one?
Will people notice mine is old?
steps.why: Xu You never asks if he can afford the empire. He asks if he needs it. One branch is a question about enough, not about money.

say: here’s what i love. xu you isn’t against having things. the bird needs its branch, the mole needs its drink. he just knows how much is enough.
in daoist teaching, an old line says it plainly: the one who knows enough is rich. not having enough. knowing it.

steps.q: Xu You also says Yao already rules well. If he took over, he’d only be after one thing. What?
steps.why: “Would I be doing it for a name?” he asks in the Zhuangzi. “Name is only the guest of reality.” He’d have the label without the substance.

today.say: before you buy or upgrade anything today, pause and ask xu you’s question: one branch, or the whole forest? if what you have is already enough, say the word inside: enough.
options: good. one branch can hold a whole nest.
lovely. then say it over what’s in reach: enough.

card.keepWhy: The one who knows enough is rich.
sources: Zhuangzi, ch. 1 (Xiaoyao you, “Free and Easy Wandering”): Yao offers the world to Xu You (when the sun and moon are out, the torches are still burning); Xu You declines: the tailorbird nests in the deep wood but uses no more than one branch; the mole drinks at the river but takes no more than a bellyful; go home, my lord, I have no use for the world. Trans. Burton Watson, The Complete Works of Chuang Tzu (1968), paraphrased.
Later telling: Xu You washes his ears in the river after Yao’s offer (Huangfu Mi, Gaoshi zhuan, 3rd century CE).
Tao Te Ching 33: 知足者富, the one who knows enough is rich (the teach’s “old line,” not named).
check: The ear-washing is a later legend, attributed here to Huangfu Mi’s Gaoshi zhuan. Confirm the source.
Yao is a legendary sage-ruler; the caption calls him “the wise emperor Yao” in “an old Daoist story.” Confirm.
The bird (jiaoliao 鷦鷯) is “tailorbird” in Watson, “wren” in other translations. Confirm.
